title: Auditor access models across Ethereum, Canton, Corda, and Rayls Enygma Public
research_question: How can financial institutions make private transactions on a public blockchain while retaining auditability and institutional control?

scope.focus: Who can read transaction data, what permission or mechanism provides access, and what the access boundary is.
exclusions: This record does not prove the configuration of a specific production Canton or Corda network.
This record does not independently decrypt an Enygma account's escrowed view key or verify the current testnet auditor account.
This record does not establish that all auditors have equivalent rights across the four systems.

sources.title: Networks
sources.version_or_scope: Ethereum public networks; page describes public network access generally and identifies Ethereum Mainnet as the primary production network.
relevant_evidence: Public networks are accessible to anyone with an internet connection.
Anyone can read or create transactions on a public blockchain and validate transactions.
supports: Ethereum public read access
does_not_support: A separate auditor role or auditor-specific permission system at Ethereum base layer.
The proposition that all information in every privacy-enabled Ethereum application is publicly readable.

sources.title: Local and external parties
relevant_evidence: An Observing Participant Node (OPN) has observation permissions for a hosted party.
The party entrusts its OPNs to record and provide read access to transactions involving that party.
A node with only observation permissions cannot submit or confirm transactions on behalf of the hosted party.
supports: Canton read-only observation permission scoped to a hosted party
does_not_support: A network-wide auditor with visibility into all Canton transactions.
Automatic access for a regulator that has not been granted the relevant party/participant relationship.

sources.title: Topology management
relevant_evidence: Observation permission means the participant node is notified only of transactions in which the hosted party is a stakeholder.
Confirmation permission includes observation; submission permission includes confirmation.
supports: Canton observation access is party-scoped and assigned through hosting topology
does_not_support: An auditor can inspect transactions unrelated to the party whose activity is observed.
Observation permission is globally read-only in every possible operational configuration beyond the documented permission semantics.

sources.title: Glossary of concepts
relevant_evidence: A contract observer is a party on a contract that can see that contract instance and its information.
Participant nodes maintain a private contract store containing contracts the participant is privy to; there is no global contract store.
Sub-transaction privacy means participants learn only the subset of a transaction in which they are directly involved.
supports: Canton contract-level observer semantics and participant-specific data visibility
does_not_support: A general-purpose regulatory auditor automatically sees every contract in a network.

sources.title: Posting transactions to observer nodes
sources.version_or_scope: Corda Enterprise 4.10 tutorial; do not silently generalize implementation details to all Corda versions.
relevant_evidence: R3 describes observer nodes as a common finance requirement where regulators want reporting on actions taken.
A regulator can run its own node and receive digitally signed, deduplicated reports.
The tutorial's application flow explicitly sends a signed transaction to a regulator and records it using ALL_VISIBLE.
supports: Corda Enterprise 4.10 application-integrated observer-node reporting to regulators
does_not_support: A Corda-wide auditor identity with automatic access to every transaction.
The assertion that every Corda application sends every transaction to every regulator by default.

sources.title: Who sees what in Enygma Public
relevant_evidence: The deployment auditor can read each shielded transaction, including sender, recipient, amount, and token.
At account registration, the wallet encrypts a copy of the view key to the deployment auditor key using ML-KEM-768 and stores it in the registry.
The auditor's view uses that key to open account view keys and display shielded transactions.
The view key does not provide spend authority; spending requires the account spend key.
The documentation says no Enygma Public contract can freeze, pause, or block funds, while also noting that the owner multisig can upgrade registry or shared-vault rules.
The page states that the Rayls team is the auditor on testnet.
supports: Enygma Public's documented deployment-level auditor mechanism
Read/decrypt capability separated from spend capability
Testnet auditor identity as an official documentation claim
does_not_support: Independent proof that the current testnet auditor actually decrypted a specific account or transaction during this review.
An immutable guarantee that freeze-related behavior can never change, because owner-multisig upgrades can change relevant contract rules.

sources.title: Enygma Public

sources.title: How Enygma Public works
relevant_evidence: The account's view key is an ML-KEM-768 key pair.
The wallet encrypts a copy of the view key to the deployment auditor key during registration.
The account's notes are readable by the owner and auditor, while the spend key remains necessary to spend notes.
supports: Technical explanation of view-key escrow and separation of read and spend authority
does_not_support: Independent cryptographic verification of the testnet auditor's private key custody or successful decryption.

sources.title: Topology
relevant_evidence: A party owner and Participant Node must consent to the hosting relationship through the relevant PartyToParticipant topology transaction.
Observation permission means the Participant Node is notified only of transactions in which the hosted party is a stakeholder.
Confirmation permission includes Observation; Submission permission includes Confirmation.

The documented topology text warns that a malicious Participant Node with Confirmation permission may submit Daml transactions in the party's name, so parties delegating Confirmation permission should sufficiently trust that node.
supports: Observation permission is party-scoped and tied to party hosting.
Observation is distinct from Confirmation and Submission.
The party owner assigns the Participant Node permission through topology.
does_not_support: A universal regulator or auditor that can read all network transactions.
Treating all observer-related permission as risk-free or equivalent to read-only.

sources.title: Privacy Model Explained — raw MDX source

relevant_evidence.text: Pattern 2: Selective Disclosure via Observers. Add specific parties as observers when they need visibility but not control. The pattern is for third parties needing visibility for compliance, audit, or information purposes. The example visibility is issuer as signatory and owner and regulator as observers; the owner is also the controller for Transfer and can execute that choice unilaterally.

Best practices include explicit auditor parties (add auditors as observers where an audit trail is required), non-consuming audit choices that return audit information, separate audit trail contracts when full visibility is not needed, and workflow patterns for temporary audit access.

supports: Canton/Daml officially documents selective observer disclosure for compliance, audit, or information purposes.
A regulator is explicitly included as an observer in the documented example.
The documentation recommends explicit auditor parties, audit choices, separate audit contracts, and time-bounded access patterns.
does_not_support: Automatic network-wide auditor access.
Proof that a particular institution has deployed these patterns in production.
Assuming all observers have no other contract rights: the documented example explicitly notes that owner is also controller for Transfer.
sources.important_limitation: The MDX lines for the headings 'Auditor as Observer' and 'Selective Audit Rights' contain component references rather than the component body content. The evidence above relies on the explicit prose in Pattern 2 and Best Practices, not on unseen component content.

sources.title: Posting transactions to observer nodes — Corda Enterprise 4.10

terminal_access.interpretation: The user's Codespace curl request was denied. This is a retrieval limitation; it does not negate the browser-accessible official documentation.

relevant_evidence: R3 says posting transactions to observer nodes is a common finance requirement where regulators may want comprehensive reporting; a regulator can run its own node and receive digitally signed, de-duplicated reports.
The TradeAndReport sample flow distributes a signed transaction to the buyer and state regulator through FinalityFlow.
The sample separately reports the transaction to the national regulator through an application flow that sends the SignedTransaction.
The regulator responder records all of the transaction's states using recordTransactions with StatesToRecord.ALL_VISIBLE.

R3 cautions that default vault queries do not distinguish states recorded as participant/owner from states recorded as observer, so custom queries should be written to return only participant/owner states where required.

When ALL_VISIBLE is used, an observer node may record all states in a transaction history that it has not already received; nodes can also contain both ALL_VISIBLE and only relevant states depending on how transactions were received.
supports: Corda Enterprise 4.10 supports application-integrated regulator reporting through observer nodes.
Regulator access is delivered through explicit transaction distribution flows rather than automatic universal visibility.
does_not_support: Every Corda application automatically reports every transaction to regulators.
A universal Corda auditor role with automatic access to all network transactions.
sources.implementation_detail: The tutorial's Kotlin and Java examples explicitly show initiateFlow(regulator), sending the signed transaction, and recordTransactions(StatesToRecord.ALL_VISIBLE, ...).
sources.evidence_lines_from_browser_open: Lines 401-409, 414-459, and 543-547 in the official R3 page.

ethereum.auditor_access_model: Public read access to public-chain data; no separate auditor-only access boundary is documented at the base network layer.
ethereum.caveat: Applications and privacy layers may keep application data or plaintext outside public ledger visibility.

canton.auditor_access_model: Two related but distinct mechanisms: (1) Daml contract observers can be explicitly assigned for selected contract-level audit visibility; (2) a party may entrust an Observing Participant Node (OPN) with Observation permission to record and provide read access to transactions involving that hosted party.
canton.scope: Daml observer: the particular contract instance and information visible under contract stakeholder rules. OPN: transactions involving the party hosted by that participant node. An Observation-only OPN cannot submit or confirm for the hosted party.
supported_patterns: The official privacy-model MDX says specific parties can be added as observers when they need visibility but not control.
It explicitly identifies compliance, audit, and information purposes, with regulator as an observer in its example.
Best practices include explicit auditor parties, non-consuming audit choices, separate audit contracts, and time-bounded workflow access.
The topology page defines Observation, Confirmation, and Submission as distinct permissions assigned by the party owner.
The official OPN page states that observation-only nodes cannot submit or confirm transactions for the parties they host.
caveats: Do not describe Canton as having an automatic network-wide auditor.
Daml contract observer rights and Participant Node Observation permission are related but distinct mechanisms.
The documentation describes capabilities and design patterns; it does not prove a named financial institution has deployed them.
The owner in the example is also a controller for Transfer; do not generalize the no-control property of the regulator observer to every observer party.
The detailed text beneath the 'Auditor as Observer' and 'Selective Audit Rights' component placeholders was not recovered from the raw MDX; do not attribute unseen details to those headings.
OPN is a party-to-participant hosting permission; do not treat it as identical to adding a Daml observer party to an individual contract.

corda.auditor_access_model: Application-integrated observer node and explicit transaction reporting flows to regulator nodes.
corda.scope: The transactions and states explicitly distributed to the regulator by CorDapp flows. The R3 Corda Enterprise 4.10 tutorial demonstrates FinalityFlow distribution to a state regulator and a separate flow that sends a signed transaction to a national regulator, whose node records states using ALL_VISIBLE.
corda.caveat: This is an application pattern, not automatic network-wide regulator visibility. The tutorial also warns that vault queries do not automatically distinguish participant/owner-recorded states from observer-recorded states.

rayls_enygma_public.auditor_access_model: Deployment auditor key used to decrypt escrowed account view keys.
rayls_enygma_public.scope: Every shielded transaction within the auditor's own deployment, according to current official product documentation.
rayls_enygma_public.caveat: A specific live decryption was not independently tested. Relevant contract rules are upgradeable by the owner multisig.

limitations_and_open_questions: Canton and Corda are permissioned deployments. Public documentation proves described capabilities, not the configuration of a named bank, regulator, or production network.
Canton contract-level Daml observer rights and Participant Node Observation hosting permission are related but distinct mechanisms.

The Canton privacy-model raw MDX contains explicit audit-pattern prose at lines 140-148 and 172-179. The body text behind the 'Auditor as Observer' and 'Selective Audit Rights' component placeholders was not retrieved, so no claims are attributed to that unseen content.
The Canton source documents a design pattern; no specific production institution's configuration or actual auditor node was independently tested.
Enygma documentation describes a deployment auditor key and escrow model, but no independent testnet decryption was performed in this review.
The fact that a view key cannot spend funds does not by itself prove that the auditor cannot correlate other public metadata or that governance rules cannot change.
Terminal hashes identify downloaded snapshots; they do not independently validate all semantic claims contained in those snapshots.

Corda Enterprise 4.10 observer-node behavior is documented by R3; terminal curl to the page returns HTTP 403, so the source was checked through browser-accessible official documentation rather than a local terminal snapshot.

The Corda tutorial illustrates explicit application-flow reporting to regulator nodes. It does not establish that all CorDapps or all Corda deployments report every transaction to a regulator by default.
